concepts.name: Rise of Hyder Ali: Path to Power in Mysore
key_dimensions: Hyder Ali's non-royal origins and rise as a military commander under the Wodeyar dynasty — a common UPSC trap on whether he was a legitimate ruler or a usurper
Administrative and military modernization: introduction of French-trained infantry and disciplined cavalry
Contrast with the Wodeyar kings: de facto vs. de jure power — relevant for comparing with later Nizam of Hyderabad's situation
Why the British initially underestimated Hyder Ali — connects to the origins of the First Anglo-Mysore War

concepts.name: First Anglo-Mysore War (1767–1769): Causes, Course, and Treaty of Madras
key_dimensions: Triple alliance against Mysore: British, Nizam of Hyderabad, and the Marathas — and why it collapsed, a frequent trick question on alliance dynamics
Hyder Ali's tactical reversal: marching to the gates of Madras, forcing a humiliating treaty on the British
Treaty of Madras (1769): mutual restitution of conquests and a defensive alliance clause — UPSC tests whether this treaty was honored by the British
Significance as the ONLY Anglo-Mysore War where the British signed a treaty on disadvantageous terms — a classic 'only' fact

concepts.name: British Betrayal of the Treaty of Madras and its Consequences
key_dimensions: British refusal to aid Hyder Ali during the Maratha invasion of Mysore (1771) — direct cause of the Second Anglo-Mysore War
How this breach of the defensive alliance clause radicalized Hyder Ali's hostility toward the British
Connecting the broken treaty to the broader pattern of British bad faith in subsidiary alliances — compare with treatment of Awadh and Hyderabad
UPSC trap: distinguishing between the Treaty of Madras (1769) and later treaties of Mangalore and Seringapatam

concepts.name: Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780–1784): Hyder Ali's Grand Alliance
key_dimensions: Formation of the confederacy: Hyder Ali, Nizam of Hyderabad, and the Marathas against the British — contrast with the collapsed triple alliance of the First War
Role of the American Revolutionary War and French intervention: how global geopolitics shaped the Carnatic theater
Battle of Pollilur (1780): most significant British defeat, where Colonel William Baillie's force was destroyed — frequently asked for its military significance
Death of Hyder Ali (December 1781) mid-war and seamless succession by Tipu Sultan — tests knowledge of continuity of Mysorean resistance

concepts.name: Treaty of Mangalore (1784): Terms, Significance, and UPSC Traps
key_dimensions: Concluded between Tipu Sultan and the British after the Second Anglo-Mysore War — the LAST treaty signed on equal terms by both parties
Mutual restitution of prisoners and conquered territories — contrast with the punitive terms imposed after the Third and Fourth Wars
Why Warren Hastings opposed the treaty: he considered it a humiliation — links to his impeachment context
UPSC trap: Treaty of Mangalore vs. Treaty of Madras — both are 'equal' treaties but in different wars; students often swap them

concepts.name: Tipu Sultan: Ideology, Administration, and Modernization
key_dimensions: Tipu's economic reforms: state trading monopolies in sandalwood, pepper, and cardamom — connects to his anti-colonial economic thinking
Military innovations: iron-cased Mysorean rockets — considered precursors to modern rocketry; frequently asked in Science & Technology context
Tipu's diplomatic outreach: embassies to France, Turkey, and Kabul — tests knowledge of his anti-British coalition-building strategy
Controversy over Tipu's religious policies: UPSC has used this to test nuanced, evidence-based historical analysis over hagiography or vilification

concepts.name: Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790–1792): Lord Cornwallis's Strategy
key_dimensions: Cornwallis's direct military command — unusual for a Governor-General; connects to the Pitt's India Act (1784) context of civil-military authority
Rebuilding the triple alliance: British, Marathas (Peshwa), and Nizam — significance of isolating Tipu diplomatically before military action
Siege of Seringapatam (1792) and its outcome: Tipu forced to sue for peace without being defeated in the field
Treaty of Seringapatam (1792): cession of half of Mysore's territory, payment of ₹3.3 crore indemnity, and giving two sons as hostages — each term is individually examinable

concepts.name: Treaty of Seringapatam (1792): Terms and Their Strategic Implications
key_dimensions: Territorial cessions: Malabar, Coorg, and Baramahal given to British; Dharwar and Raichur to Marathas; Guntur to Nizam — UPSC tests which territory went to which power
The hostage clause: Tipu's sons Abdul Khaliq and Muiz-ud-Din taken to Madras — humanizing detail often used in Mains answers
Financial indemnity as a tool of economic weakening — compare with indemnity clauses in Treaty of Lahore (1846) after First Anglo-Sikh War
How the treaty weakened but did not destroy Tipu — setting up the inevitability of the Fourth War under Wellesley

concepts.name: Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799): Lord Wellesley and the Doctrine of Subsidiary Alliance
key_dimensions: Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance System as the ideological driver of the war — Tipu's refusal to accept it as the proximate cause
Tipu's diplomatic efforts to seek French alliance in the context of Napoleon's Egyptian campaign — the geopolitical trigger for British preemptive action
The fall of Seringapatam (May 4, 1799) and death of Tipu Sultan — 'Tiger of Mysore' symbolism frequently used in Mains
UPSC trap: Wellesley used the pretext of Tipu's 'treacherous' French correspondence — tests students on distinguishing pretext from actual cause

concepts.name: Fall of Seringapatam and Death of Tipu Sultan (1799)
key_dimensions: Military details: role of treachery by Mir Sadiq (Tipu's diwan) in opening the breach — connects to internal subversion as a recurring British strategy
Arthur Wellesley's (future Duke of Wellington) role in the siege — his formative experience in India; relevant for British imperial history
Tipu's symbolic significance: his death as the end of independent Indian resistance in the south
Post-battle treatment of Tipu's family: sons reinstated as pensioners; contrast with brutal treatment of defeated rulers elsewhere — nuanced Mains point

concepts.name: Restoration of the Wodeyar Dynasty and the Mysore Residency
key_dimensions: British restored the Wodeyar dynasty (Krishna Raja Wadiyar III) — UPSC trap: Mysore was NOT annexed directly after 1799, unlike other conquered territories
Mysore placed under a Subsidiary Alliance — loss of sovereignty despite nominal independence
The Mysore Residency as an instrument of British control: compare with Hyderabad and Awadh residencies
Later annexation of Mysore (1831) by British due to alleged misgovernance — then restored in 1881 as a 'model native state'; tests long-arc historical thinking

concepts.name: Role of the Nizam of Hyderabad in the Anglo-Mysore Wars
key_dimensions: The Nizam switched sides between wars: allied with Mysore in First War, against Mysore in Third and Fourth Wars — tests understanding of shifting alliances
Why the Nizam aligned with the British ultimately: fear of Maratha power over fear of British expansion
Nizam's territorial gains from Third War (Guntur region) — how the British used territorial rewards to consolidate allies
The Nizam accepting Subsidiary Alliance (1798) just before the Fourth War — connecting the Anglo-Mysore conflict to the broader Subsidiary Alliance narrative

concepts.name: Role of the Marathas in the Anglo-Mysore Wars
key_dimensions: Marathas allied with Hyder Ali initially (Second War) but switched sides for the Third and Fourth Wars — the instability of Maratha-Mysore relations
Peshwa Madhav Rao I's earlier defeat of Hyder Ali (1764–1767) as background context for Maratha-Mysore rivalry
How the British exploited the Maratha-Mysore rivalry to isolate Tipu — a masterclass in 'divide and rule'
Post-1799: With Mysore neutralized, British attention shifted to the Marathas — the Anglo-Mysore Wars as the precursor to the Anglo-Maratha Wars

concepts.name: French Factor in the Anglo-Mysore Wars
key_dimensions: French alliance with Hyder Ali during the Second War: Battle of Cuddalore (1783) as a French naval victory — yet the Treaty of Paris (1783) neutralized French gains
Tipu's embassy to France (1787) and recruitment of French officers for his army
Napoleon's Egyptian campaign (1798–99) and Tipu's letters seeking French alliance — British used this to justify preemptive war
UPSC trap: French support was more diplomatic and symbolic than materially decisive in any of the four wars — tests nuanced evaluation

concepts.name: Governor-Generals and Their Roles Across the Four Wars
key_dimensions: First War: Lord Verelst/Madras Council — decentralized command; Second War: Warren Hastings — strategic oversight but military failure initially
Third War: Lord Cornwallis — personal field command, notable for a Governor-General leading troops; contrast with his administrative reforms
Fourth War: Lord Wellesley — used Subsidiary Alliance as the framework; aggressive forward policy
UPSC frequently asks: 'Which Governor-General was associated with which Anglo-Mysore War?' — a direct factual trap

concepts.name: Mysorean Rockets: Military Technology and Legacy
key_dimensions: Iron-cased rockets with bamboo poles used by Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan — superior to British technology of the era
William Congreve's development of the Congreve Rocket after studying Mysorean rockets captured in 1799 — direct technological transfer
UPSC Science & Technology angle: Tipu Sultan credited as a pioneer of rocket artillery in modern warfare
Rockets displayed at the Royal Artillery Museum, London — an often-cited fact in India's scientific heritage context

concepts.name: Economic Dimensions of the Anglo-Mysore Conflict
key_dimensions: Mysore's control over Malabar pepper and cardamom trade: a key British commercial motivation for war
Tipu's state-controlled trading monopolies as a direct challenge to East India Company's commercial interests
War indemnities (especially 1792) as tools of economic strangulation: how reparations weakened Mysore between wars
Post-1799 exploitation of Mysore's resources under the Residency system — connects to drain of wealth theory

concepts.name: Comparison of All Four Anglo-Mysore Wars: Causes, Outcomes, and Treaties
key_dimensions: A structured comparative framework: First (British humiliation/Treaty of Madras) → Second (stalemate/Treaty of Mangalore) → Third (British victory/Treaty of Seringapatam) → Fourth (decisive British victory/no treaty, annexation)
Progressive shift in power balance: from Mysore's strength in First and Second Wars to British dominance in Third and Fourth
UPSC trap: Only the First and Second Wars ended with treaties favorable to or equal for Mysore; Third and Fourth were punitive
Pattern question: 'How did the Anglo-Mysore Wars contribute to British paramountcy in India?' — requires synthesis across all four wars

concepts.name: Tipu Sultan's Diplomatic Outreach and Coalition-Building Strategy
key_dimensions: Embassies to France (1787), Ottoman Turkey (1787), and Afghanistan (Zaman Shah) — attempts to build an anti-British pan-Islamic or European alliance
Why these alliances failed: French Revolution disrupted France; Zaman Shah was preoccupied with Persia; Ottomans were distant
UPSC trap: Tipu's outreach is sometimes romanticized as proto-nationalist — examiners test whether students can critically evaluate its actual effectiveness
Wellesley's use of Tipu's French correspondence as justification for the Fourth War — the difference between diplomatic contact and actual military alliance

concepts.name: Legacy and Historical Significance of the Anglo-Mysore Wars
key_dimensions: Anglo-Mysore Wars as the turning point for British supremacy in South India — after 1799, no major southern power could challenge the British
Tipu Sultan's legacy in Indian nationalist historiography: from 'freedom fighter' to contested figure — UPSC Mains tests ability to present multiple perspectives
Strategic lessons: how the wars demonstrated the effectiveness of the Subsidiary Alliance System as a tool of conquest without direct annexation
Connection to subsequent British expansion: the removal of Mysore threat enabled the Anglo-Maratha Wars (1803, 1817) — tests ability to link events in a causal chain
